subtype: Approach: using helplines and emergency services when danger is immediate [Action]
passage: I'm Bhupen, and I live above the stationery shop, so I see most of what happens on our lane. Tuesday evening Vikas came out of the gully with his phone against his ear, walking so fast he nearly hit my cycle. He was saying, "Papa, come now, it's Ashwin, my best friend, he says he doesn't want to be here anymore, he's at his flat." Then he put his father on hold and dialled the emergency number. He gave the flat number and the building name twice, slowly. He did not run off to Ashwin's himself. When his father's scooter turned in, Vikas pointed and they left together. I couldn't tell whether he was frightened or just sure of what to do. His hands were shaking, but his voice was not. Later his father told me Ashwin was safe and his parents were with him.

qa.q: What did Vikas do after he put his father on hold?
qa.a: He dialled the emergency number and gave the flat number and the building name twice, slowly.

qa.q: How can you tell that Vikas was frightened but steady, and how sure can Bhupen be?
qa.a: His hands were shaking but his voice was not, so he seemed scared yet sure of what to do, though Bhupen admits not being able to tell for certain.

qa.q: If Vikas could not reach his father, what else could he do, and why?
qa.a: He could call a mental health helpline or another adult nearby along with the emergency number, because immediate danger needs adults and trained responders, not a teen alone.

qa.q: How might Ashwin see Vikas's quick calls later?
qa.a: Ashwin may feel frightened or embarrassed, yet also cared for, since a friend acted at once and adults reached him.

grounding: A teen calls a family adult and the emergency number at once when a friend is in immediate danger, seen through a bystander's eyes.

subtype: Approach: using helplines and emergency services when danger is immediate [Action]
passage:
Monday, in October: At a school session, the counsellor writes two things on the board: the emergency number, and a mental health helpline. “If someone you know is in danger right now, you don't handle it alone. Wake an adult. Call.” Kishore saves both in his phone.
Saturday, three weeks later, 11:40 pm: A message from Saurabh: “sorry for everything. bye.” Then Saurabh's phone goes off. Kishore's hands shake. He doesn't try to sort it out by text. He runs to his parents' room and wakes his father. Papa calls the emergency number and gives Saurabh's address; Kishore calls the helpline and follows what they tell him, while Papa drives the two of them to Saurabh's building. An ambulance is already there, and Saurabh's parents are with him.
Wednesday: Saurabh is safe and getting help. Kishore goes to see the school counsellor too, because he still can't sleep.

qa.q: What two things did the counsellor write on the board?
qa.a: The emergency number and a mental health helpline.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling when Saurabh's message came?
qa.a: Kishore was terrified, hands shaking, but knew not to try to handle it alone by text.

qa.q: Why was waking Papa and calling for help better than texting Saurabh back?
qa.a: It was an emergency, and only adults and emergency services could reach Saurabh in time; texting alone would have lost minutes.

qa.q: How might that week feel for Kishore's father?
qa.a: Papa was probably frightened that night but relieved Kishore woke him at once, and glad Kishore is also seeing the counsellor.

grounding: Shows a teen who, when a friend is in immediate danger, wakes a parent and calls the emergency number and a helpline at once instead of handling it alone.

subtype: Approach: using helplines and emergency services when danger is immediate [Action]
passage:
Sangeeta, you asked why I made you save those two numbers. Let me tell you about one night when I was sixteen.
My friend Farida called me very late. She was crying and saying things that frightened me, that she couldn't do this any more, that she was sorry. I remember wanting to fix it myself: talk her round, promise to visit tomorrow. I was her best friend; I thought that was my job.
But something in her voice told me tomorrow was too late. I kept her talking on the phone, and with my other hand I shook my Ammi awake. Ammi took one look at my face and called the emergency number, then Farida's family, while I stayed on the line with Farida until they reached her.
She's alive, Sangeeta. She has children now. I didn't save her; the adults and the doctors did. My job was to call them fast.
So your Zeenat Khala says: those numbers stay in your phone.

qa.a: The emergency number, then Farida's family.

qa.q: What was young Zeenat feeling during Farida's call?
qa.a: Zeenat was frightened, and at first felt a strong pull to fix it alone as the best friend.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the difference?
qa.a: Waking Ammi while keeping Farida on the line, so adults called emergency help at once instead of waiting till tomorrow.

qa.q: How might Ammi have felt being woken that night?
qa.a: Ammi was probably shocked and scared, but acted immediately, and was likely proud of her daughter afterwards.

grounding: An elder recalls a night when a friend was in immediate danger and she woke her mother, who called the emergency number, rather than handling it alone.
